title: Firmware rollout
like: an over-the-air update for a million smart devices
brief: A new firmware goes out to a million smart devices at 03:00 when they are idle. Every device asks "is there an update?", then downloads the same file in pieces, then reports back. If they all wake together, they can flatten your service, and a device that fails to update must not be left broken.

clarify.q: Do all devices need the update at once?
clarify.a: No. Within a few hours is fine, so the rush can be spread out.

clarify.q: Are the files the same for everyone?
clarify.a: Yes, per model. The same pieces are asked for by hundreds of thousands of devices.

clarify.q: What if a device keeps failing?
clarify.a: It keeps its old firmware and tries again later. The service must tell us how many devices updated.

notes: The firmware is about 40 MB, cut into 1 MB pieces (approx.).
Devices wake together in the first minutes after 03:00 (approx.).
One app server handles about 1,000 requests a second (approx.).

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

numbers.label: Piece requests per second at the start
Share served from the edge copy
numbers.how: Everyone asks for the same pieces, so an edge copy answers nearly all of them (approx.)

hints: A million devices ask for the same few files. What should answer them, and what should never see them?
A CDN with a long copy time serves the pieces. The small "is there an update" and "I finished" calls need a rate limiter and a stream so they cannot flood the database.
Serving capacity does not establish firmware safety; staged rollout needs a measured stop rule. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: The firmware pieces never change, so the edge serves them. The small status calls are the part that can hurt: a rate limiter and a stream take the wall of reports and let the database fill at its own pace.

designs.name: Edge pieces, rate-limited status calls
designs.why: The CDN keeps each piece for a week and the shield collapses misses into one trip to object storage. Status calls pass a rate limiter and land on an event stream, which a small worker group writes into the key-value store at a steady pace.

tradeoffs: Rolling out to a few percent first catches a bad firmware before it reaches everyone, at the price of a slower rollout.
Random delays on each device spread the rush for free, and cost nothing on the server side.
A rate limiter protects the database, but devices that are turned away must back off, not retry at once.
A week-long edge copy needs a new file name for each version, so devices never read a stale piece.
editorial.realWorld: Large device makers stage updates over days and rely on edge networks, because a million devices asking at once would otherwise look like an attack (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Firmware rollout: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Stage signed firmware and stop safely when devices fail the rollout. Complete bytes do not prove authenticity or compatibility. Rollback-safe activation needs a recovery slot or equivalent durable protocol. Serving capacity does not establish firmware safety; staged rollout needs a measured stop rule.

fields.label: Step 1. A device downloads all pieces of version V. May it boot immediately?
options: Verify signed manifest, checksum and compatibility, then atomically activate
Boot once the download byte count matches
fields.explanation: Complete bytes do not prove authenticity or compatibility.

fields.label: Step 2. The device loses power during installation. What boots next?
options: A validated previous image or recoverable installation state
fields.explanation: Rollback-safe activation needs a recovery slot or equivalent durable protocol.

fields.label: Step 3. The canary cohort exceeds its failure threshold. What follows?
options: Continue because the CDN has capacity
Stop expansion and roll back compatible devices while retaining diagnostics
fields.explanation: Serving capacity does not establish firmware safety; staged rollout needs a measured stop rule.

correctness.responsibility: Stage signed firmware and stop safely when devices fail the rollout.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 1500 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $3187. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
